notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Sound is a form of mechanical energy transmitted through a material medium as a wave.
  • Sound is produced by vibrating objects.
  • Sound requires a material medium for propagation.
  • Sound cannot travel through vacuum.
  • Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases.
  • Sound generally travels fastest in solids and slowest in gases.
  • In air, sound travels mainly as a longitudinal wave.
  • Sound transfers energy without permanent bulk transport of matter.
  • The branch of physics dealing with sound is called acoustics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sound → Vibration + Medium + Mechanical Wave

2. Production of Sound
  • Sound is produced when an object vibrates.
  • A vibrating tuning fork produces sound.
  • Vocal cords vibrate during speech.
  • A stretched string vibrates in string instruments.
  • A drum membrane vibrates when struck.
  • An air column vibrates in wind instruments.
  • Sound stops when vibration producing it stops.
3. Vibration
  • Vibration is repeated motion about a mean or equilibrium position.
  • A vibrating body transfers energy to neighbouring particles.
  • These particles transfer disturbance to adjacent particles.
  • The disturbance propagates as a sound wave.
4. Sound Requires a Medium
  • Sound cannot propagate through a perfect vacuum.
  • A material medium is required because sound is a mechanical wave.
  • Gas molecules transmit sound through pressure variations.
  • Liquids transmit sound through molecular interactions.
  • Solids transmit sound through elastic vibrations.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Light → Can travel through vacuum.

Sound → Cannot travel through vacuum.

5. Bell-Jar Experiment
  • A ringing electric bell can be placed inside a bell jar.
  • As air is removed, sound becomes weaker.
  • The bell can still be seen vibrating.
  • This demonstrates that sound requires a material medium.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bell Jar → Sound Needs Medium

6. Longitudinal Wave
  • In a longitudinal wave, particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation.
  • Sound in air is longitudinal.
  • Longitudinal sound waves contain compressions and rarefactions.
  • Particle displacement is back-and-forth along the direction of travel.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sound in Air → Longitudinal

7. Compression
  • Compression is a region of high pressure and high particle density in a longitudinal wave.
  • Particles are relatively closer together in a compression.
  • Compressions travel through the medium with the wave.
8. Rarefaction
  • Rarefaction is a region of lower pressure and lower particle density.
  • Particles are relatively farther apart.
  • Compressions and rarefactions alternate in a sound wave.
📌 Remember

Compression → High pressure

Rarefaction → Low pressure

9. Transverse Wave
  • In a transverse wave, particle vibration is perpendicular to wave propagation.
  • Waves on a stretched string can be transverse.
  • Electromagnetic waves such as light are transverse.
  • Ordinary sound waves in gases are not transverse.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Sound in air → Longitudinal.

Light → Transverse electromagnetic wave.

10. Wave Terms

Important sound-wave quantities are:

  • Amplitude.
  • Frequency.
  • Time period.
  • Wavelength.
  • Wave speed.
  • Phase.
11. Amplitude
  • Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a vibrating particle from its mean position.
  • Greater amplitude generally produces greater sound intensity.
  • Loudness is related to amplitude and human perception.
  • Energy carried by a wave generally increases strongly with amplitude.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Amplitude ↑ → Intensity ↑ → Usually louder

12. Frequency
  • Frequency is the number of complete vibrations per second.
  • Frequency is represented by f.
  • SI unit is hertz.
  • One hertz means one vibration or cycle per second.
  • Frequency primarily determines pitch.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Frequency → Pitch

13. Time Period
  • Time period is the time required for one complete vibration.
  • It is represented by T.
  • SI unit is second.
  • T = 1/f.
  • f = 1/T.
📌 Remember

fT = 1

14. Wavelength
  • Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive points in the same phase.
  • In a longitudinal wave, it may be measured between successive compressions.
  • It can also be measured between successive rarefactions.
  • Wavelength is represented by λ.
  • SI unit is metre.
15. Wave Speed
  • Wave speed relates frequency and wavelength.
  • v = fλ.
  • v is wave speed.
  • f is frequency.
  • λ is wavelength.
  • When sound enters another medium, frequency remains determined by the source while speed and wavelength may change.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

v = fλ

16. Speed of Sound in Air
  • Speed of sound in dry air at about 20°C is approximately 343 m/s.
  • A common textbook approximation is 340 m/s.
  • Speed of sound in air increases with temperature.
  • It is faster in warm air than in cold air.
📌 Remember

Sound in air ≈ 340–343 m/s near room temperature

17. Effect of Temperature
  • Speed of sound in gases increases as temperature increases.
  • Warmer gas molecules move faster.
  • Near ordinary temperatures, sound speed in air increases by roughly 0.6 m/s for each 1°C rise.
  • Temperature strongly affects atmospheric sound propagation.
18. Effect of Humidity
  • Sound travels slightly faster in humid air than in dry air at the same temperature.
  • Water vapour lowers the average molar mass of air.
  • This increases sound speed slightly.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Humid air → Sound travels slightly faster than in dry air.

19. Speed in Different Media

General order:

  • Solids → Fastest.
  • Liquids → Intermediate.
  • Gases → Slowest.
  • Sound speed depends on elasticity and density of the medium.
  • Strong elastic restoring forces generally increase wave speed.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Solid > Liquid > Gas

20. Sound in Steel and Water
  • Sound travels much faster in steel than in air.
  • Sound also travels faster in water than in air.
  • This explains why vibrations can sometimes be detected through rails or water before airborne sound arrives.
21. Pitch
  • Pitch is the sensation that allows a sound to be judged as high or low.
  • Pitch mainly depends on frequency.
  • Higher frequency produces higher pitch.
  • Lower frequency produces lower pitch.
  • Pitch is a perceptual property.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

High Frequency → High Pitch

22. Loudness
  • Loudness is the perceived strength of sound.
  • It depends mainly on sound intensity, frequency and sensitivity of the ear.
  • Greater amplitude generally produces greater loudness.
  • Loudness is subjective.
  • Intensity is an objective physical quantity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Loudness ≠ Intensity exactly.

23. Quality / Timbre
  • Timbre or quality distinguishes sounds having the same pitch and similar loudness.
  • Timbre depends on waveform and harmonic content.
  • A violin and flute can sound different even when playing the same note.
  • Overtones contribute strongly to timbre.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Timbre → Distinguishes Sound Sources

24. Sound Intensity
  • Sound intensity is sound power transmitted per unit area.
  • SI unit is watt per square metre.
  • Intensity generally decreases as distance from a point source increases.
  • For an ideal point source, intensity follows an inverse-square relation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Intensity → W/m²

25. Inverse-Square Law for Sound
  • For an ideal point source in open space, intensity varies approximately as 1/r².
  • Doubling distance reduces intensity to about one-fourth.
  • Tripling distance reduces intensity to about one-ninth.
26. Decibel
  • Sound level is commonly expressed in decibels.
  • Symbol is dB.
  • The decibel scale is logarithmic.
  • Sound-intensity level β = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀).
  • I₀ is a reference intensity.
  • The standard reference intensity in air is 10⁻¹² W/m².
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Reference Intensity → 10⁻¹² W/m²

27. Zero Decibel
  • 0 dB does not mean absence of sound.
  • It corresponds approximately to the standard reference intensity near the threshold of human hearing at suitable frequencies.
  • Negative dB values are possible relative to the standard reference.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

0 dB ≠ Absolute silence.

28. Increase of 10 dB
  • An increase of 10 dB corresponds to ten times the sound intensity.
  • An increase of 20 dB corresponds to 100 times the intensity.
  • The decibel scale is logarithmic, not linear.
29. Audible Range of Humans
  • Typical young human hearing ranges from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
  • 20,000 Hz = 20 kHz.
  • Hearing range usually decreases with age, especially at high frequencies.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Human Audible Range → 20 Hz to 20 kHz

30. Infrasonic Sound
  • Infrasound has frequency below 20 Hz.
  • It is normally below human hearing range.
  • Elephants can produce and detect low-frequency sounds.
  • Earthquakes and volcanic activity can generate infrasonic waves.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Infrasound → < 20 Hz

31. Ultrasonic Sound
  • Ultrasound has frequency above 20 kHz.
  • It is above the normal upper limit of human hearing.
  • Ultrasound has important medical and industrial applications.
  • Dogs, bats and dolphins can detect frequencies above the normal human range.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ultrasound → > 20 kHz

32. Animals and Ultrasound
  • Bats use high-frequency sound for echolocation.
  • Dolphins use echolocation.
  • Dogs hear higher frequencies than humans.
  • Some insects also detect ultrasonic frequencies.
33. Echolocation
  • Echolocation uses emitted sound and returning echoes to determine the position of objects.
  • Bats use echolocation during navigation and hunting.
  • Dolphins use echolocation underwater.
  • The time delay of echoes gives distance information.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Echolocation → Sound + Echo + Distance

34. Reflection of Sound
  • Sound can be reflected from surfaces.
  • Hard, large surfaces reflect sound strongly.
  • Soft porous materials tend to absorb sound.
  • Reflection follows geometric laws similar to reflection of other waves under suitable conditions.
  • Echo and reverberation arise from reflected sound.
35. Laws of Reflection of Sound
  • Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
  • Incident sound, reflected sound and normal lie in the same plane.
  • Smooth large surfaces can produce strong reflected sound.
36. Echo
  • Echo is a reflected sound heard separately from the original sound.
  • The human ear generally needs a time gap of about 0.1 s to distinguish two sounds separately.
  • For sound speed about 343 m/s, a reflecting surface should be roughly 17 m or more away for a distinct echo under ideal conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Distinct Echo Distance → About 17 m

37. Echo Formula
  • Sound travels to the reflector and back.
  • Total distance travelled = 2d.
  • Therefore d = vt/2.
  • d is distance to reflector.
  • v is speed of sound.
  • t is round-trip echo time.
📌 Must-Memorise

Distance = Speed × Time / 2

38. Reverberation
  • Reverberation is persistence of sound due to multiple reflections after the source stops.
  • Excessive reverberation reduces speech clarity.
  • Auditoriums are designed to control reverberation.
  • Absorbing materials reduce unwanted reflections.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Echo → Distinct reflected sound.

Reverberation → Persistence due to repeated reflections.

39. Reducing Reverberation
  • Curtains absorb sound.
  • Carpets absorb reflected sound.
  • Acoustic tiles reduce reflections.
  • Cushioned seats absorb sound.
  • False ceilings and porous panels improve acoustics.
40. Acoustics
  • Acoustics is the science of sound.
  • Architectural acoustics studies sound behaviour in buildings.
  • Good auditorium design balances adequate loudness and controlled reverberation.
  • Sound-absorbing and reflecting surfaces are selected carefully.
41. SONAR
  • SONAR stands for Sound Navigation and Ranging.
  • It uses sound waves to detect underwater objects and determine distance.
  • SONAR commonly uses ultrasonic frequencies.
  • A pulse is transmitted.
  • Returning echo is detected.
  • Time interval is used to calculate distance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

SONAR → Sound Navigation and Ranging

42. SONAR Formula
  • Depth or distance d = vt/2.
  • v is speed of sound in water.
  • t is total time for sound to travel to object and return.
  • Division by 2 accounts for two-way travel.
43. Uses of SONAR
  • Measuring ocean depth.
  • Locating submarines.
  • Detecting underwater obstacles.
  • Fish finding.
  • Mapping the seabed.
  • Underwater navigation.
44. Ultrasound in Medical Imaging
  • Ultrasound imaging uses high-frequency sound waves.
  • A transducer emits and receives ultrasound.
  • Reflected echoes are converted into images.
  • Ultrasound does not use ionising X-rays.
  • It is widely used in obstetric and abdominal imaging.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ultrasound Imaging → Echoes, not X-rays

45. Doppler Ultrasound
  • Doppler ultrasound measures changes in frequency caused by moving blood cells.
  • It can assess blood flow.
  • It applies the Doppler effect.
  • It is used in vascular and cardiac examinations.
46. Ultrasound Cleaning
  • Ultrasonic cleaners produce high-frequency vibrations in liquids.
  • Cavitation and fluid motion help remove dirt from small surfaces.
  • They are used for jewellery, instruments and precision components.
47. Ultrasound in Industry
  • Ultrasound can detect internal cracks in metal components.
  • Reflected waves reveal discontinuities.
  • It is used in non-destructive testing.
  • Ultrasonic thickness measurement is also widely used.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ultrasound → Non-Destructive Testing

48. Ultrasonic Lithotripsy
  • High-energy sound waves can be used in certain procedures to break kidney stones.
  • The fragments can then pass more easily or be removed.
  • The technique is called lithotripsy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lithotripsy → Breaking Stones using Shock/Sound Waves

49. Doppler Effect
  • Doppler effect is the apparent change in frequency due to relative motion between source and observer.
  • If source and observer approach each other, observed frequency increases.
  • If they move apart, observed frequency decreases.
  • Christian Doppler proposed the effect in 1842.
  • Doppler effect occurs for sound and electromagnetic waves.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Approaching → Frequency ↑

Receding → Frequency ↓

50. Examples of Doppler Effect
  • Pitch of an approaching ambulance siren appears higher.
  • Pitch drops as the ambulance moves away.
  • Doppler radar measures speed.
  • Doppler ultrasound measures blood flow.
  • Astronomical redshift and blueshift are related Doppler/cosmological phenomena.
51. Resonance
  • Resonance occurs when a system is driven at or near its natural frequency.
  • Oscillation amplitude can become large.
  • Musical instruments use resonance.
  • Resonance boxes amplify sound.
  • Excessive resonance can damage structures.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Resonance → Driving Frequency ≈ Natural Frequency

52. Natural Frequency
  • Natural frequency is the frequency at which a system tends to vibrate when disturbed.
  • Different objects can have different natural frequencies.
  • Resonance occurs when external forcing matches a natural frequency.
53. Tuning Fork
  • A tuning fork produces a nearly pure tone.
  • It vibrates at a characteristic frequency.
  • Tuning forks are used for tuning musical instruments.
  • Frequency of a tuning fork is usually stamped on it.
  • Standard concert pitch commonly uses A4 = 440 Hz.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tuning Fork → Known Frequency

54. Resonance Box
  • A tuning fork sounds louder when placed on a resonance box.
  • The box forces a larger volume of air to vibrate.
  • This increases radiated sound intensity.
55. Forced Vibration
  • Forced vibration occurs when an object is made to vibrate by an external periodic force.
  • Frequency of forced vibration follows the driving frequency.
  • Resonance is a special case when driving frequency is close to natural frequency.
56. Free Vibration
  • Free vibration occurs after a system is displaced and released without continuous external periodic driving.
  • The system vibrates near its natural frequency.
  • Friction gradually reduces amplitude in real systems.
57. Damped Vibration
  • Damping causes oscillation amplitude to decrease with time.
  • Friction and air resistance produce damping.
  • Shock absorbers use damping.
  • Acoustic materials can damp sound vibrations.
58. Beats
  • Beats occur when two sounds of slightly different frequencies interfere.
  • Loudness rises and falls periodically.
  • Beat frequency = |f₁ − f₂|.
  • Musicians use beats while tuning instruments.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Beat Frequency → |f₁ − f₂|

59. Interference of Sound
  • Sound waves obey the principle of superposition.
  • Constructive interference produces greater amplitude.
  • Destructive interference produces reduced amplitude.
  • Noise-cancelling headphones use destructive interference principles.
60. Standing Waves
  • Standing waves form by interference of two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions.
  • Nodes have minimum displacement.
  • Antinodes have maximum displacement.
  • Standing waves occur in strings and air columns.
  • Musical instruments use standing-wave patterns.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Node → Minimum displacement

Antinode → Maximum displacement

61. Fundamental Frequency
  • Fundamental frequency is the lowest natural frequency of a vibrating system.
  • It is also called the first harmonic.
  • Higher natural frequencies are called overtones or harmonics depending on the system.
62. Harmonics
  • Harmonics are frequencies that are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency in ideal harmonic systems.
  • Second harmonic = 2f₁.
  • Third harmonic = 3f₁.
  • Harmonics affect timbre.
63. Overtones
  • Overtones are resonant frequencies above the fundamental.
  • The first overtone is the next frequency above the fundamental.
  • In many ideal strings and open pipes, first overtone is the second harmonic.
  • In a closed pipe, first overtone is the third harmonic.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

First overtone is not always second harmonic.

64. Vibrating String
  • A stretched string produces sound when it vibrates.
  • Frequency depends on length.
  • Frequency depends on tension.
  • Frequency depends on mass per unit length.
  • Shorter strings produce higher frequencies.
  • Greater tension produces higher frequencies.
  • Heavier strings produce lower frequencies.
65. Frequency of Stretched String

For an ideal stretched string:

  • f = 1/(2L) √(T/μ).
  • L is vibrating length.
  • T is tension.
  • μ is mass per unit length.
📌 Remember

Length ↓ → Frequency ↑

Tension ↑ → Frequency ↑

Mass per length ↑ → Frequency ↓

66. String Instruments
  • Violin.
  • Guitar.
  • Veena.
  • Sitar.
  • Piano strings.
  • Pitch is controlled by changing string length, tension or mass per unit length.
67. Wind Instruments
  • Wind instruments produce sound through vibrating air columns.
  • Flute.
  • Clarinet.
  • Trumpet.
  • Nadaswaram.
  • Pipe organ.
  • Pitch depends mainly on effective length of the vibrating air column.
68. Open Pipe
  • An open pipe is open at both ends.
  • Both ends are displacement antinodes in the simple model.
  • Fundamental wavelength λ = 2L.
  • Fundamental frequency f = v/2L.
  • Open pipes can support all integer harmonics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Open Pipe → All Harmonics

69. Closed Pipe
  • A closed pipe is closed at one end and open at the other.
  • Closed end is a displacement node.
  • Open end is a displacement antinode.
  • Fundamental wavelength λ = 4L.
  • Fundamental frequency f = v/4L.
  • Ideal closed pipes support odd harmonics only.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Closed Pipe → Odd Harmonics

70. Open vs Closed Pipe
  • Open pipe fundamental → f = v/2L.
  • Closed pipe fundamental → f = v/4L.
  • For equal length, open-pipe fundamental is twice the closed-pipe fundamental.
71. Drum
  • A drum produces sound from a vibrating stretched membrane.
  • Striking the membrane sets it into vibration.
  • Air around the membrane transmits the sound.
  • Membrane vibration patterns are more complex than those of ideal strings.
72. Tabla and Mridangam
  • Tabla and mridangam are percussion instruments.
  • Sound is produced by vibrating membranes.
  • The loading and construction of the membrane affect overtones and tone quality.
  • They produce complex harmonic structures.
73. Human Voice
  • Human voice is produced mainly by vibration of vocal folds in the larynx.
  • Air from lungs passes through the vocal folds.
  • Vocal-fold tension and length affect pitch.
  • Mouth, throat and nasal cavities act as resonators.
  • Tongue and lips shape speech sounds.
74. Human Ear

Main parts:

  • Outer ear.
  • Middle ear.
  • Inner ear.
  • The ear converts sound waves into nerve impulses.
  • The brain interprets these impulses as sound.
75. Outer Ear
  • Pinna collects sound waves.
  • External auditory canal guides sound to the eardrum.
  • The eardrum is also called tympanic membrane.
  • Sound waves make the tympanic membrane vibrate.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pinna → Collects Sound

76. Tympanic Membrane
  • Tympanic membrane separates outer ear from middle ear.
  • It vibrates in response to sound.
  • Its vibrations are transmitted to the middle-ear bones.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Eardrum → Tympanic Membrane

77. Ear Ossicles

The three small bones of the middle ear are:

  • Malleus.
  • Incus.
  • Stapes.
  • They transmit and amplify vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear.
  • Stapes is the smallest bone in the human body.
📌 Must-Memorise

Malleus → Incus → Stapes

78. Stapes
  • Stapes is commonly called the stirrup bone.
  • It is the smallest bone in the human body.
  • It transmits vibration to the oval window of the inner ear.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Smallest Human Bone → Stapes

79. Eustachian Tube
  • Eustachian tube connects the middle ear with the throat region.
  • It helps equalise air pressure on both sides of the eardrum.
  • Swallowing during air travel can help equalise pressure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Eustachian Tube → Pressure Equalisation

80. Cochlea
  • Cochlea is a spiral-shaped structure in the inner ear.
  • It contains sensory structures involved in hearing.
  • Vibrations produce fluid movements inside the cochlea.
  • Hair cells convert mechanical vibrations into electrical nerve signals.
  • The auditory nerve carries signals toward the brain.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cochlea → Hearing

81. Organ of Corti
  • The organ of Corti lies within the cochlea.
  • It contains sensory hair cells.
  • Hair-cell movement leads to auditory nerve signals.
  • Damage to hair cells can cause permanent hearing loss.
82. Semicircular Canals
  • Semicircular canals are part of the inner ear.
  • They help detect rotational head movement.
  • They are important for balance and equilibrium.
  • They are not primarily responsible for hearing.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cochlea → Hearing.

Semicircular canals → Balance.

83. Auditory Nerve
  • The auditory or cochlear nerve carries hearing information from cochlea to brain.
  • It forms part of the vestibulocochlear nerve, cranial nerve VIII.
84. Hearing Process — Sequence

Sound wave →

  • Pinna.
  • Ear canal.
  • Tympanic membrane.
  • Malleus.
  • Incus.
  • Stapes.
  • Oval window.
  • Cochlea.
  • Hair cells.
  • Auditory nerve.
  • Brain.
📌 Must-Memorise Sequence

Pinna → Eardrum → Ossicles → Cochlea → Auditory Nerve

85. Hearing Loss
  • Conductive hearing loss involves problems transmitting sound through outer or middle ear.
  • Sensorineural hearing loss involves damage to inner-ear structures or auditory pathways.
  • Excessive sound exposure can damage cochlear hair cells.
  • Hearing loss can be temporary or permanent depending on cause.
86. Hearing Aid
  • Hearing aids amplify and process sound.
  • A microphone converts sound into electrical signals.
  • Electronics process/amplify the signal.
  • A receiver converts the signal back into sound.
  • Hearing aids assist many people with hearing loss.
87. Cochlear Implant
  • A cochlear implant is an electronic medical device.
  • It can directly stimulate the auditory nerve electrically.
  • It may help some people with severe sensorineural hearing loss.
  • It does not simply amplify sound like a conventional hearing aid.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Hearing aid → Amplifies sound.

Cochlear implant → Electrical stimulation of auditory nerve.

88. Noise
  • Noise is unwanted or unpleasant sound.
  • Noise can interfere with communication and sleep.
  • Prolonged excessive noise can damage hearing.
  • Noise pollution is an environmental problem.
89. Noise Pollution

Major sources include:

  • Road traffic.
  • Aircraft.
  • Railways.
  • Construction.
  • Industrial machinery.
  • Loudspeakers.
  • Generators.
  • Firecrackers.
90. Effects of Noise Pollution
  • Hearing impairment.
  • Sleep disturbance.
  • Reduced concentration.
  • Stress responses.
  • Interference with communication.
  • Reduced quality of life.
  • Wildlife can also be affected by excessive anthropogenic noise.
91. Noise-Control Measures
  • Maintain vehicles and machinery.
  • Use silencers and mufflers.
  • Use sound barriers.
  • Install acoustic insulation.
  • Control unnecessary horn use.
  • Maintain green belts where appropriate.
  • Separate noisy industrial activities from sensitive areas where planning permits.
92. Soundproofing
  • Soundproofing reduces sound transmission between spaces.
  • Dense barriers reduce transmission.
  • Porous materials absorb reflected sound.
  • Double glazing reduces sound transmission through windows.
  • Air gaps and insulation can improve sound isolation.
93. Musical Sound
  • Musical sounds generally have regular or structured vibrations.
  • Definite pitch may be present.
  • Harmonics produce characteristic timbre.
  • Musical quality depends on frequency spectrum and envelope.
94. Noise vs Musical Sound
  • Noise often has irregular, broad-spectrum vibration.
  • Musical tone often has periodic components.
  • The distinction also depends on perception and context.
  • A sound considered music by one listener may be unwanted noise to another.
95. Mach Number
  • Mach number compares object speed with local speed of sound.
  • Mach number M = Object speed / Local speed of sound.
  • Mach 1 means speed equal to sound speed.
  • Mach number has no unit.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mach 1 → Speed of Sound

96. Subsonic Motion
  • Subsonic means speed below the local speed of sound.
  • Mach number is less than 1.
97. Supersonic Motion
  • Supersonic means speed greater than local speed of sound.
  • Mach number is greater than 1.
  • Supersonic aircraft produce shock waves.
98. Hypersonic Motion
  • Hypersonic commonly refers to speeds of Mach 5 and above.
  • Aerodynamic heating becomes very significant at such speeds.
  • Shock-wave effects become important.
99. Shock Wave
  • A shock wave is a sharp pressure disturbance.
  • It forms when an object moves faster than the local speed of sound.
  • Pressure changes occur abruptly across the shock.
  • Supersonic aircraft generate shock waves.
100. Sonic Boom
  • Sonic boom is the loud sound associated with shock waves from a supersonic object.
  • It is not produced only at the instant an aircraft crosses Mach 1.
  • A continuously supersonic aircraft generates a moving shock-wave pattern.
  • Observers hear the boom when the shock wave passes them.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Sonic boom is associated with supersonic shock waves, not merely one single “breaking of sound barrier” event.

101. Sound Barrier
  • “Sound barrier” is a historical term describing aerodynamic difficulties encountered near the speed of sound.
  • It is not a physical wall.
  • Modern aircraft can be designed to cross the transonic region safely.
102. Sound in Space
  • Space is nearly a vacuum.
  • Ordinary mechanical sound cannot travel through vacuum.
  • Astronauts communicate using radio waves.
  • Radio waves are electromagnetic and can travel through vacuum.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Astronaut Communication → Radio Waves, not Sound through vacuum

103. Thunder and Lightning
  • Light travels much faster than sound.
  • Therefore, lightning is seen before thunder is heard.
  • Sound speed in air is about 340 m/s.
  • Light speed is about 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
  • Time delay can be used to estimate approximate distance to lightning.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lightning seen first → Light much faster than sound

104. Estimating Lightning Distance
  • If thunder is heard about 3 seconds after seeing lightning, the event is roughly 1 km away.
  • This is an approximate rule because sound speed varies with atmospheric conditions.
  • Light travel time over a few kilometres is negligible compared with sound travel time.
105. Seismic Waves — Sound Link
  • Seismic waves are mechanical waves travelling through Earth.
  • P-waves are longitudinal.
  • S-waves are transverse.
  • P-waves travel through solids and liquids.
  • S-waves do not propagate through liquids.
  • Seismic-wave behaviour helped reveal Earth's internal structure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

P-wave → Longitudinal → Solid + Liquid

S-wave → Transverse → Solid only

106. P-Waves
  • P stands for primary.
  • P-waves are compressional longitudinal waves.
  • They are the fastest seismic body waves.
  • They arrive first at seismic stations.
  • They can pass through solids and liquids.
107. S-Waves
  • S stands for secondary.
  • S-waves are transverse shear waves.
  • They are slower than P-waves.
  • They cannot travel through liquids.
  • Their absence through Earth's outer core supports the conclusion that the outer core is liquid.
108. Acoustic Devices
  • Stethoscope transmits body sounds.
  • SONAR uses reflected sound underwater.
  • Ultrasound scanner uses echoes.
  • Microphone converts sound to electrical signal.
  • Loudspeaker converts electrical signal to sound.
  • Hearing aid amplifies sound.
109. Stethoscope
  • A stethoscope is used to listen to internal body sounds.
  • It transmits vibrations from chest piece through tubing to the ears.
  • Heart and lung sounds are commonly examined.
  • Modern electronic stethoscopes may amplify and filter signals.
110. Microphone
  • A microphone converts sound energy into electrical signals.
  • Different microphones use different transduction principles.
  • Dynamic microphones use electromagnetic induction.
  • Condenser microphones use changes in capacitance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Microphone → Sound to Electrical

111. Loudspeaker
  • A loudspeaker converts electrical signals into sound.
  • Current in a voice coil interacts with a magnetic field.
  • The coil moves a cone or diaphragm.
  • The vibrating diaphragm creates sound waves.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Loudspeaker → Electrical to Sound

112. Alexander Graham Bell
  • Alexander Graham Bell is strongly associated with development and patenting of the telephone.
  • The telephone converts sound into electrical signals and reproduces sound at the receiving end.
  • Bell's work was important in the development of telecommunications.
113. Christian Doppler
  • Christian Doppler was an Austrian physicist.
  • He proposed the Doppler effect in 1842.
  • The effect describes frequency change due to relative motion.
  • It has applications in astronomy, radar and medical ultrasound.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Doppler → 1842 → Frequency Shift

114. Heinrich Hertz
  • Heinrich Hertz experimentally demonstrated electromagnetic waves.
  • The SI unit of frequency, hertz, is named after him.
  • One hertz means one cycle per second.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hertz → Frequency Unit

115. Ernst Chladni
  • Ernst Chladni studied vibrating plates and acoustic patterns.
  • Chladni figures reveal nodal patterns on vibrating plates.
  • He is sometimes called a father of experimental acoustics.
116. Important Sound Formulae
  • Wave speed → v = fλ.
  • Frequency → f = 1/T.
  • Time period → T = 1/f.
  • Echo distance → d = vt/2.
  • Sound level → β = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀).
  • Beat frequency → |f₁ − f₂|.
  • Mach number → Object speed / Sound speed.
  • Stretched string → f = 1/(2L)√(T/μ).
  • Open pipe fundamental → f = v/2L.
  • Closed pipe fundamental → f = v/4L.
117. Important Units
  • Frequency → Hertz.
  • Time period → Second.
  • Wavelength → Metre.
  • Sound speed → m/s.
  • Intensity → W/m².
  • Sound level → Decibel.
  • Mach number → No unit.
118. Must-Memorise Sound Pairs
  • Frequency → Pitch.
  • Amplitude → Intensity/loudness.
  • Timbre → Quality.
  • Infrasound → Below 20 Hz.
  • Audible → 20 Hz–20 kHz.
  • Ultrasound → Above 20 kHz.
  • Echo → Reflection.
  • SONAR → Ultrasound/echo.
  • Doppler → Frequency shift.
  • Resonance → Matching frequency.
  • Beat → Difference frequency.
  • Cochlea → Hearing.
  • Semicircular canals → Balance.
  • Stapes → Smallest bone.
  • Eustachian tube → Pressure equalisation.
119. TNPSC Traps
  • Sound is mechanical.
  • Light is electromagnetic.
  • Sound cannot travel in vacuum.
  • Sound in air is longitudinal.
  • Sound generally travels fastest in solids.
  • Frequency determines pitch.
  • Amplitude is strongly related to intensity and loudness.
  • Timbre distinguishes sounds of same pitch.
  • Frequency unit is hertz.
  • Decibel is logarithmic.
  • 0 dB is not absolute silence.
  • Human audible range is approximately 20 Hz–20 kHz.
  • Infrasound is below 20 Hz.
  • Ultrasound is above 20 kHz.
  • Echo requires sufficient time delay.
  • Distinct echo distance is roughly 17 m in air at room temperature.
  • SONAR distance formula contains division by 2.
  • Ultrasound imaging does not use ionising X-rays.
  • Doppler effect changes observed frequency.
  • Approaching source gives higher observed frequency.
  • Beat frequency is the difference of two frequencies.
  • Closed pipe supports odd harmonics in the ideal model.
  • Pinna collects sound.
  • Tympanic membrane is the eardrum.
  • Stapes is the smallest bone.
  • Cochlea is primarily for hearing.
  • Semicircular canals are primarily for balance.
  • Eustachian tube equalises pressure.
  • Sonic boom is caused by shock waves.
  • Astronauts do not hear ordinary sound through vacuum.
  • P-waves pass through liquids.
  • S-waves do not pass through liquids.
120. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Sound → Mechanical wave.
  • Source → Vibration.
  • Vacuum → No sound.
  • Air sound → Longitudinal.
  • Compression → High pressure.
  • Rarefaction → Low pressure.
  • v → fλ.
  • Frequency → Pitch.
  • Amplitude → Loudness.
  • Timbre → Quality.
  • Audible → 20–20,000 Hz.
  • Infra → <20 Hz.
  • Ultra → >20 kHz.
  • Echo → Reflection.
  • Echo distance → vt/2.
  • Reverberation → Multiple reflections.
  • SONAR → Underwater echo.
  • Doppler → Frequency shift.
  • Resonance → Frequency match.
  • Beats → |f₁−f₂|.
  • Open pipe → All harmonics.
  • Closed pipe → Odd harmonics.
  • Pinna → Collects.
  • Eardrum → Vibrates.
  • Ossicles → Malleus, Incus, Stapes.
  • Cochlea → Hearing.
  • Semicircular canals → Balance.
  • Stapes → Smallest bone.
  • Mach 1 → Sound speed.
  • Supersonic → > Mach 1.
  • Sonic boom → Shock waves.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What produces sound? → Vibrating objects.
  • Nature of sound? → Mechanical wave.
  • Does sound require a medium? → Yes.
  • Can sound travel through vacuum? → No.
  • Sound in air is mainly? → Longitudinal wave.
  • Regions of high pressure in sound wave? → Compressions.
  • Regions of low pressure? → Rarefactions.
  • Wave-speed formula? → v = fλ.
  • SI unit of frequency? → Hertz.
  • One hertz means? → One cycle per second.
  • Frequency determines? → Pitch.
  • Higher frequency gives? → Higher pitch.
  • Amplitude mainly affects? → Sound intensity and perceived loudness.
  • Property distinguishing two instruments playing same note? → Timbre.
  • SI unit of sound intensity? → W/m².
  • Sound level commonly measured in? → Decibel.
  • Is decibel scale linear? → No, logarithmic.
  • Reference sound intensity? → 10⁻¹² W/m².
  • Does 0 dB mean complete silence? → No.
  • Normal human audible range? → About 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
  • Frequency below 20 Hz? → Infrasound.
  • Frequency above 20 kHz? → Ultrasound.
  • Animal well known for ultrasonic echolocation? → Bat.
  • Another echolocating animal? → Dolphin.
  • General speed order of sound? → Solid > Liquid > Gas.
  • Approximate speed of sound in room-temperature air? → About 343 m/s.
  • Does sound travel faster in warm or cold air? → Warm air.
  • Does sound travel slightly faster in humid or dry air? → Humid air.
  • Reflection of sound producing distinct repeat? → Echo.
  • Approximate minimum reflector distance for distinct echo? → About 17 m.
  • Echo-distance formula? → d = vt/2.
  • Persistence caused by repeated reflections? → Reverberation.
  • How is reverberation reduced? → Sound-absorbing materials.
  • Science of sound? → Acoustics.
  • SONAR stands for? → Sound Navigation and Ranging.
  • SONAR mainly uses? → Sound echoes, commonly ultrasound.
  • SONAR depth formula? → d = vt/2.
  • Medical ultrasound uses? → High-frequency sound waves and echoes.
  • Does ultrasound imaging use X-rays? → No.
  • Ultrasound used to detect cracks in metals? → Yes.
  • Technique for breaking kidney stones with shock/sound waves? → Lithotripsy.
  • Apparent frequency change due to motion? → Doppler effect.
  • Approaching source produces? → Higher observed frequency.
  • Receding source produces? → Lower observed frequency.
  • Scientist associated with Doppler effect? → Christian Doppler.
  • Year associated with Doppler proposal? → 1842.
  • Large vibration when driving frequency matches natural frequency? → Resonance.
  • Instrument producing nearly pure known tone? → Tuning fork.
  • Beat-frequency formula? → |f₁ − f₂|.
  • Standing-wave point of zero/minimum displacement? → Node.
  • Point of maximum displacement? → Antinode.
  • Lowest natural frequency? → Fundamental frequency.
  • First harmonic equals? → Fundamental frequency.
  • Stretched-string frequency increases when length? → Decreases.
  • String frequency increases when tension? → Increases.
  • String frequency decreases when mass per unit length? → Increases.
  • Open-pipe fundamental? → v/2L.
  • Closed-pipe fundamental? → v/4L.
  • Ideal open pipe supports? → All integer harmonics.
  • Ideal closed pipe supports? → Odd harmonics.
  • Voice produced mainly by? → Vocal-fold vibration.
  • Part of ear that collects sound? → Pinna.
  • Eardrum scientific name? → Tympanic membrane.
  • Three middle-ear bones? → Malleus, Incus and Stapes.
  • Smallest human bone? → Stapes.
  • Structure mainly responsible for hearing? → Cochlea.
  • Sensory structure in cochlea? → Organ of Corti.
  • Structures mainly responsible for balance? → Semicircular canals.
  • Tube equalising middle-ear pressure? → Eustachian tube.
  • Nerve carrying hearing information? → Auditory/cochlear nerve.
  • Hearing aid mainly does? → Amplifies/processes sound.
  • Cochlear implant mainly does? → Electrically stimulates auditory nerve.
  • Unwanted sound? → Noise.
  • Prolonged excessive noise can damage? → Cochlear hair cells/hearing.
  • Mach number means? → Object speed divided by local sound speed.
  • Mach 1 means? → Speed of sound.
  • Below Mach 1? → Subsonic.
  • Above Mach 1? → Supersonic.
  • Mach 5 and above commonly called? → Hypersonic.
  • Cause of sonic boom? → Shock waves.
  • Can ordinary sound travel in space vacuum? → No.
  • How do astronauts communicate? → Radio waves.
  • Why is lightning seen before thunder is heard? → Light travels far faster than sound.
  • Approximate rule for lightning distance? → About 1 km for every 3 seconds of thunder delay.
  • P-wave type? → Longitudinal/compressional.
  • S-wave type? → Transverse/shear.
  • Which seismic wave travels through liquids? → P-wave.
  • Which cannot travel through liquids? → S-wave.
  • Microphone converts? → Sound to electrical signal.
  • Loudspeaker converts? → Electrical signal to sound.
  • Unit hertz named after? → Heinrich Hertz.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Sound → Mechanical; Air → Longitudinal; v = fλ; Pitch → Frequency; Loudness → Amplitude/Intensity; Echo → Reflection; SONAR → vt/2; Human hearing → 20 Hz–20 kHz.
